Q2 FY27 Earnings Conference Call Transcript 
October 16, 2026 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Urban Company Limited 
October 16, 2026 
 
Moderator 
Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome to Urban Company Limited’s Q2 FY27 
Earnings Conference Call.  
We have Mr Abhiraj Singh Bhal, CEO & Co-founder and Mr Abhay Mathur, Chief 
Financial Officer from the Urban Company management team on the call today. 
As a reminder, all participant lines will be in the listen-only mode and there will be an 
opportunity for you to ask questions after the management's remarks.  
Please note that this call is being recorded and the audio call and the transcript will be 
available on the company's website.  
Additionally, please note that this earnings call is scheduled for a duration of 45 minutes. If 
you wish to ask a question, please use the raise hand feature available on your Zoom 
dashboard. We will announce your name on the call and unmute your line post which you 
can proceed with your question.  
Our results and shareholder letters have been published to the exchanges and uploaded on 
the company's IR website.  
Before we begin the call, I would like to remind all the attendees that some statements or 
comments made on the call today by the management can be deemed as forward-looking 
and hence may involve certain risks and uncertainties. Such statements or comments are 
not guarantees of future performance and the actual results may differ.  
Over to Mr Abhiraj Singh Bhal for the opening remarks. 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Thank you, Bhavya. 
Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Urban Company's Q2 FY27 earnings call. 
Ladies and gentlemen, we have now completed one full year as a listed company, and it has 
been a year of strong growth and solid execution. Every segment of our business has scaled 
well, growth has stepped up, and Q2 only saw that momentum continuing further. 
On a consolidated basis, net transaction value grew 39.1% year-on-year to reach ₹1,432.3 
crores, and revenue from operations grew 41.4% year-on-year to reach ₹537.3 crores. Our 
orders delivered more than doubled year-on-year to reach 15.1 million, and annual 
transacting users grew 34.5% to reach almost 10 million. 
Adjusted EBITDA loss recorded was ₹144 crores, but this reflected a ₹174 crore 

investment in InstaHelp. Excluding InstaHelp, adjusted EBITDA was ₹30 crores positive, 
up 213% year-on-year. 
For the purposes of this call, we want to share three key messages with the investor and 
analyst community. 
First, our growth has stepped up structurally, and every business has a very long runway for 
growth. Consolidated NTV has grown by almost 40% for three straight quarters, well ahead 
of our pre-listing trend. That growth comes from faster new user acquisition, which has 
been up 46.3% over this period, better repeat behaviour, which keeps us compounding, and 
densification of our micro-markets, which makes our services faster, cheaper, and better. 
India Consumer Services, our core business, grew 26.3% year-on-year in the current 
quarter, Q2. I might remind our listeners that this growth has come off a tougher base — 
Q2 last year was 900 basis points higher in year-on-year growth compared to Q1 last year. 
Further, the festive season this year is falling entirely into Q3. So we're quite happy with 
the 26.3% year-on-year growth. 
More importantly, in the India Consumer Services business, we feel that our penetration 
runway is very large. For our largest categories, in our top 8 cities, penetration continues to 
be well below 10%, and our Tier 2 cities are now growing much faster and becoming a 
strong second engine for growth. 
Coming to our international markets, we grew at 66.2% year-on-year. UAE is a very large 
market for us, and despite the war, it has continued to grow very well, and all concerns 
around growth in that market are now well and truly behind us. 
Native recorded another strong quarter of growth, with 35.4% year-on-year growth. This 
was despite the festive sales moving completely into Q3. We expect the overall 
year-on-year growth of Q2 and Q3 put together to be in the range of 50% to 55%. 
In InstaHelp, we continue to be aggressive. Orders grew 63% quarter-on-quarter to reach 
6.23 million, and in the micro-markets of InstaHelp, which run alongside our core business, 
about 45% of all new users to the platform now come through InstaHelp. 
So that was the first point — that growth has materially stepped up. It is structural, and 
every business, in our view, has now got a long runway for growth. 
Second, the growth is driving operating leverage. The core is now profitable, with 
expanding margins year-on-year, and we are investing aggressively in InstaHelp by choice. 
Adjusted EBITDA, excluding InstaHelp, was at ₹30 crores this quarter, up 213% 
year-on-year, and ₹119 crores for the past three quarters, up 175% year-on-year. During Q2 
FY27, India Consumer Services saw a margin improvement of 110 basis points 
year-on-year to reach 3.5%. International saw a 190 basis points margin improvement 
year-on-year to reach 2% of NTV, and Native's loss margin narrowed by 220 basis points 
year-on-year. 
Even in InstaHelp, where we continue to make meaningful investments as a deliberate 
choice to cement our market leadership, the unit economics improved with density, and loss 
per order fell 19% quarter-on-quarter, from ₹346 to ₹279. 

So that's the second point we want to reiterate — which is that our core businesses are now 
getting more profitable, with expanding margins, driven by the operating leverage that 
growth provides. And we are investing aggressively in InstaHelp by choice. 
The third and last point is that we are firmly on track to achieving the targets that we had 
set out for ourselves, and we are raising capital for strategic flexibility. 
We closed the quarter with ₹1,901 crores of cash and treasury investments on our balance 
sheet, and a core business that generated ₹119 crores of adjusted EBITDA over the past 
three quarters. 
Our businesses now are materially larger than they were at the time of listing. Growth has 
stepped up, and we now operate three businesses at scale with proven economics. 
The proposed raise of up to ₹2,500 crores is about flexibility. It lets us invest with 
conviction across each of these business lines, cement our leadership in InstaHelp, and 
pursue inorganic opportunities selectively, without trading off one for the other. 
I want to underscore that we believe we are firmly on track to achieve our adjusted 
EBITDA breakeven goal by Q3 FY28, and we are very confident, now more than ever 
before, of achieving the ₹1,000 crores adjusted EBITDA goal that we set out for FY31. 
With that, we'd be happy to take questions from the analyst community. Thank you. 
Moderator 
Thank you, Abhiraj. We will now wait for the question queue to assemble. As a reminder, if 
you wish to ask a question, please use the raise hand feature available on your Zoom 
dashboard. We will announce your name on the call and unmute your line, post which you 
can proceed with your questions. 
The first question is from the line of Mr Gaurav Rateria from Morgan Stanley. Please go 
ahead. 
Gaurav Rateria 
I hope I'm audible. 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yes, good evening. 
Gaurav Rateria 
Yeah, hi, congrats on great execution. I have a couple of questions. For the India Core 
Consumer Services, the instant proposition has really helped — probably to get better 
repeat, higher frequency and lower churn. But what is driving the higher pace of new 
customer acquisition, and how sustainable is it? 
My second question is on average spend per customer, which historically has grown at 
6–7% year-on-year. It's come out a little slower in the current quarter, at 3%, so anything to 
read into this number. And the last question is on your foray into the residential AC 
segment — it would be great to get a little bit of thought on our edge and right to win, as 
far as the product is concerned and as far as the distribution capabilities are concerned. 
Thank you. 

Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Thank you, Gaurav, for your questions. Let me start with India Core. You're right, the 
growth has continued to remain very healthy, and it is driven, in large part, by both new 
user acquisition as well as our cohorts and repeat base compounding well. 
I think on the new user acquisition side, it's a combination of three things, Gaurav. One is, 
of course, the proposition itself has become stronger for customers. With densification, 
what we are able to do is deliver our services faster under UC Instant, and increasingly 
now, consumers are able to see, in the top 7–8 cities, services available within the hour, and 
very often within 30 minutes or so. 
Secondly, we've continued to make meaningful investments in training, in SOPs, in tooling, 
and quality control via AI, and that compounds the word of mouth faster, which is the 
biggest source of acquisition for us from a new user standpoint. 
And third, in pockets, we have also leveraged the utilization improvements that we have 
driven to give more value to users in terms of better pricing. So I think the underlying 
proposition has strengthened, and that has helped us. 
The second factor that is driving acceleration for new users is Tier 2 markets. As we have 
mentioned in the letter as well, Tier 2 is now growing much faster, and I think it's a 
function of Tier 2 users essentially getting a wider assortment of services now available to 
them, and our own focus on Tier 2 markets in the past few quarters has increased — we've 
started to double down, and we will continue to do that for the coming years ahead. 
And finally, we've stepped up on customer marketing as well, and that would have been 
visible in the India Core P&L that we've drawn out. So, a combination of all three things 
has stepped up new users. We are very confident of this trajectory continuing — we see a 
long growth runway, as I mentioned at the start of the call as well. 
On average spend, I think there's nothing material to talk about. It's a combination of some 
mix change, a little bit of the festive season moving further along this year, and, in pockets, 
as I mentioned, we've passed on the benefits of densification to consumers. 
On the residential AC side, our view is that we've now operated in the segment of air 
conditioning servicing and repair for close to 11–12 years, ever since the inception of the 
company, and there's a lot of data and knowledge that we have gathered on what are the 
consumer pain points, and what are some of the unmet needs of the consumers. 
Based on those data points and our own understanding of the market and the unmet needs, 
we have been quietly working on creating an innovative, cutting-edge product. We will be 
very calibrated and measured in terms of this particular endeavour and the rollout of this. 
We expect the next year or two to be more about learning, and mostly from a channel 
standpoint as well — I think we will limit it largely to our app. So the idea is to learn in the 
first year or two, to get feedback from consumers. 
We believe we are on track to launching an air conditioner device that will be very, very 
innovative, and much like all our other products in Native, will bring a breath of fresh air to 
the category. But at the same time, we want to be very calibrated and measured in the way 
we approach this. Native has been doing very well — growth has been strong, and margins 
have been improving, and we now believe we're within touching distance of profitability in 
Native, and we would like that trajectory to continue. So our foray into AC should not 

materially change that trajectory. 
Gaurav Rateria 
Thank you, all the best. 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Thank you. Thank you. 
Moderator 
Thank you. Next question is from the line of Mr Manish Adukia from Goldman Sachs. 
Please go ahead. 
Manish Adukia 
Hi, good evening. Thank you for taking my questions. I also have three questions, and 
maybe my first question would be on the use of proceeds from the announced potential 
capital raise. When you mentioned that you may also potentially look at some acquisitions 
or inorganic opportunities, can you maybe provide some colour in which part of your 
business or segment you would need to build capability through M&A? And second, when 
you think about M&A, could these be bolt-on acquisitions? How are you thinking about the 
range or scale of what kind of target you may look to acquire? That's my first question. 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yep. Manish, so, as I mentioned in the opening remarks, the purpose of this fundraise is 
predominantly to ensure that we have strategic flexibility over the next 5 to 10 years, and 
that we have a strong balance sheet to execute on our vision, which is to build a much, 
much larger company than we are today. In fact, we still believe we're a very small 
company in the scheme of things, and our ambition is to go beyond being just a home 
services company and eventually become the trusted home platform for Indian consumers 
— almost the operating system for the Indian home. 
So, given that ambition, we want the strategic flexibility over the next few years to invest in 
all our areas of business, whether it's India Core, International, Native, and InstaHelp. Each 
of them plays a distinctly important role, and we think that this fundraise, of up to ₹2,500 
crores, will significantly strengthen the balance sheet and give us that flexibility. 
We've talked about inorganic opportunities as well, and I would say in India Core, Native, 
and our international markets, the ecosystem around us has evolved. There is nothing 
imminent, but we will always be open and look out for the right opportunities, and if there 
is an attractive opportunity at the right valuation that we believe can be meaningfully 
additive to the company and create long-term shareholder value, we are very much open to 
doing that. So that, I think, is our current thought process. 
Manish Adukia 
Thank you, Abhiraj. If I may just ask a follow-on on that — on your India Core Services, 
where you are by far the market leader, or probably the only player out there, and you're a 
multi-category platform — could there be any possibility of acquisition in that vertical? I'm 
just trying to understand what you might need through M&A in your core services, where 
you already have multiple categories, so I'm just trying to get some flavour, even if 
qualitatively, as to what kind of capabilities you would want to build through M&A, if at all 
you're able to share that. 

Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yeah, so it's a good question, and I think maybe I'll take the question one level higher and 
answer it more at a framework level. So, I think the framework we will use is: either an 
M&A should allow us to consolidate a particular market that we find ourselves in, or it 
should allow us to enter a new category or market. 
Now, given that, we've explicitly said in the past as well that we don't look to enter any new 
countries. For India Core, if at all we do an M&A, it would be to add on categories that we 
don't operate in today, where we feel that the decision of build versus buy may be tilting in 
favour of buying, provided things are accretive from a valuation standpoint. So I would say 
that's the broad framework we would look at. We would look at a similar framework within 
our other lines of business as well. 
Manish Adukia 
Very clear, thank you, Abhiraj. My second question — of course, when you look at 
InstaHelp as a business, the net order value continues to come down, and I'm assuming that 
versus what you would have thought two or three quarters ago, the competitive intensity 
has probably remained elevated for a prolonged period of time. But despite that, like you 
said, you remain confident of delivering on your break-even target of Q3 of next fiscal year. 
Is that a function of your core businesses, including International and Native, doing that 
much better versus your own expectations in terms of profitability, and that's why you 
remain confident of delivering break-even at a company level? Or do you think how things 
evolve in InstaHelp in the next one or two quarters will actually determine whether you get 
there or not — just trying to get a sense of whether, despite that, you could still deliver 
break-even if competition remains high in InstaHelp? 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yes, so Manish, I think why we remain confident on achieving the Q3 FY28 break-even 
goal at a consolidated level is a function of two things. One, I think the growth trajectory 
and the operating leverage that growth brings to our three main businesses — India Core, 
International, and Native — is strong, and certainly much stronger and much ahead of what 
our expectations were a year back, at the time of the IPO and in the first earnings call when 
we set out these targets. So that gives us significant additional cushion, I would say — and 
not just incremental, additional cushion. 
Two, in InstaHelp — and I want to reiterate this point — I don't think the losses are high 
because of competitive intensity. The losses are high because we are choosing to keep them 
high, and we are choosing to invest from a position of strength, because we have a certain 
view on the TAM, the opportunity, and how we would like to play it. 
And since the beginning of this year, we have been executing on a certain plan, with 
deliberation, and that plan we have drawn out pretty much all the way for the next 6 to 8 
quarters. Now, you're obviously in a competitive environment, reacting tactically to 
ongoing situations, but at the highest level, I think it's not that we are reacting to 
competitive intensity — if anything, our aggression is what the others have to keep up with. 
So, we have a certain plan in place, we're executing on that plan, and we believe that that 
plan will fructify into both us achieving the targets that we've set out to achieve, as well as 
cementing our leadership position in InstaHelp. 

Manish Adukia 
Thank you, Abhiraj, very clear. And just my last question is a follow-on to your response to 
Gaurav's question earlier on the potential foray into air conditioners — thank you for 
providing colour that the next one to two years would be like a learning phase, but again, 
still trying to understand — when you look at your various businesses, all of them are 
doing really well from a growth perspective: India Core, like you said, is accelerating, Tier 
2 is seeing good traction there, InstaHelp, of course, is competitive and you're also 
investing there, International has again accelerated — so all businesses are doing well. And 
in that waterfall, when Native is yet not profitable — yes, it's getting there, but still not 
profitable — and other businesses may also potentially require some growth investments, 
and they're doing well, why choose a new category to enter into when so many other parts 
of the business are doing well, and may do even better if you continue to invest there? So 
just trying to understand, from a capital allocation waterfall perspective, how does air 
conditioning take priority, or where does that fit in terms of the amount of allocation that it 
may see? 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yeah. So, in our view, Native is well and truly on track to achieve its profitability goals — I 
think it will actually happen pretty soon, and that's part of the reason why we think, from a 
timing perspective, it's the right time as well. 
And our own view, from a capital allocation standpoint, is that we want to be fairly 
disciplined in the build-up of AC. Like I said, once Native is profitable, we want that 
trajectory to continue — we don't want a foray into AC to, in any way, deviate from that 
trajectory. 
In fact, we've mentioned in the letter as well that R&D expenses in Native are today the 
bulk of the EBITDA losses, so from that, one can derive where the underlying profitability 
is already tracking. 
Finally, an entry into any new category is a function of — one doesn't think about just the 
next few quarters, but takes a very long-term view. In the long term, we believe this is a 
very attractive category for Native. We do almost 10 times more air conditioner servicing, 
repair and installation orders compared to water purifiers, and the category is also perhaps 
10 times larger in terms of TAM. And there are genuine pain points which, over the last 
10–12 years of building this category from a servicing standpoint, we have seen consumers 
experience. 
And we will be very calibrated, measured, learn, go slow, and set this business up for 
long-term success. I don't think we're looking at any immediate numbers in the first one or 
two years — I think it's all about keeping things in a learning phase, and thinking about 
how we succeed over the next 5 to 10 years from that long-term picture perspective. I 
would say it can become a fairly strong pillar for Native. 
Manish Adukia 
Thank you, Abhiraj. Really appreciate your responses and insight. All the best. 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Thank you, Manish. 

Moderator 
Thank you, Manish. Our next question is from the line of Mr Sachin Salgaonkar from Bank 
of America. Please go ahead. 
Sachin Salgaonkar 
Hi, thank you for the opportunity. Abhiraj, a really big-picture question to think about, and 
this is what I'm trying to grapple with — you guys had always maintained a stance that 
Urban Company doesn't need cash, that you have a good amount of cash on your balance 
sheet. So trying to understand what has now changed, which is now leading to dilution to 
shareholders. I understand from your comments today that competition at InstaHelp has not 
changed — while it is intense, it has not increased — and I also understand growth has 
stepped up, and there is operating leverage coming through on the back of it. But yet, when 
I look at your FY31 target, it's unchanged, right? So how should we think about the capital 
being raised — will it be invested for growth, and hence, should we see upside to that 
FY31 EBITDA target? 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Good question, Sachin. See, we are very clear that this capital is being raised for strategic 
flexibility, and predominantly for growth. I think from a build-out of our existing organic 
businesses, as well as InstaHelp, to be honest, the trajectory that we are on, the current 
balance sheet is more than sufficient — and if it was not, we would have changed the short- 
to medium-term targets, but those remain unchanged. 
So we believe that the additional capital is not necessarily to fund the losses in InstaHelp, 
or for the short-term needs that the other businesses might have, but more from a 
longer-term perspective — to provide strategic cushion, and definitely to look at any 
interesting inorganic opportunities, which, given where Insta's trajectory is, the current 
balance sheet does not provide that level of strategic flexibility for. 
And absolutely, as and when we do invest, these investments will be growth investments, 
and they should result in a higher trajectory of top line and bottom line in the medium to 
long term — which is one of the reasons why I underscored that we remain extremely 
confident of that long-term target of ₹1,000 crores by FY31. And if I'm saying that out on 
the earnings call, then obviously internally, our assumptions would be much, much higher. 
Sachin Salgaonkar 
Yeah, sorry to stick on this point, but the question I'm trying to get at is, why now? Because 
you're saying that you need capital, let's say, from a 10-year point of view, where your core 
consumer business clearly has EBITDA increasing, and there is that guidance of roughly 
100 basis points improvement in margin every quarter. So clearly, with the accelerated 
growth, as well as things improving, you do see that incremental cash coming in. Native — 
you're saying the business, despite the foray into ACs, will remain on a profitable 
trajectory. International is also increasing. And InstaHelp is what you guys are choosing to 
invest in. So, in that context, clearly you do have that flexibility — so what do you mean by 
incremental flexibility, what you want, and why now from a capital raise point of view? 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yeah, no, that's a good question, Sachin. I think — see, there's never a perfect time to do 
these things. The very definition of flexibility is that the sooner you do it, the more 
flexibility you have. 

I think today, for instance, I wouldn't say that we enjoy a lot of flexibility from the current 
balance sheet standpoint, given where Insta's losses are, and the other requirements. So, at 
this point in time, the current balance sheet allows us to execute precisely on the plan that 
we have laid out for ourselves in an organic fashion. 
I think the incremental capital allows us to be more aggressive, to see newer opportunities 
that may come along, to look at inorganic acquisitions more closely, and, in the worst-case 
scenario, if the TAM, for instance, is significantly larger than we are envisaging, and the 
competitive intensity dramatically increases, it gives us the option to play on the front foot, 
without being defensive. That's about it. 
Sachin Salgaonkar 
Got it. And last question from my side is, when you say you're open to acquisitions, ideally, 
should we also think about a potential acquisition into the InstaHelp category — where, 
let's say, interest rates in the US are such that it's not easy for anyone to raise incremental 
capital, and you guys are sitting on a good amount of cash — is that an M&A opportunity 
you guys are also open to exploring? 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
So, I'd never say never, but it's highly unlikely. 
Sachin Salgaonkar 
Cool, alright, thank you. 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Thank you. 
Moderator 
Thank you. Our next question is from the line of Mr Abhishek Pathak from Motilal Oswal. 
Please go ahead. 
Abhishek Pathak 
Yeah, hi, am I audible? 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yes, please go ahead. 
Abhishek Pathak 
Hi, Abhiraj, congrats on another good quarter. My question is on the perspective of supply 
of experts as well as helps. On the InstaHelp side, do you think, in the near to medium 
term, the supply or the recruitment of helps becomes a rate limiter on growth? And to  that 
effect, if somebody — should somebody choose to invest or should somebody kind of you 
know  — come in and offer slightly better take rates to our experts and our helps, how do 
we safeguard against that, and does that impact growth in any way? 
And the second question, again on the InstaHelp side, is: do we have a working, 
unit-economics steady-state picture that we have in mind, that we aim to achieve in the next 
two to three years? I understand it may be a high single-digit EBITDA business, but in 
terms of sacrificing those margins for the next three to four years, do we believe that more 
interventions would lead to outsized growth? Because the TAM that we've put out still kind 
of limits the ceiling to which InstaHelp can grow — so how do those investments pan into 

that whole situation? Thank you. 
Abhiraj Singh Bhal 
Yep. So, Abhishek, in terms of the availability of supply — and this answer is true as much 
for InstaHelp as it is for the rest of our business — I would differentiate between 
availability of people and the ability to recruit, train, onboard, and retain the right skill and 
talent from a long-term perspective. 
So, people are available — I don't think there's a shortage of that, especially if the earnings 
proposition is strong, and we've given out our latest update on the Earnings Index, where 
you can see that the earnings proposition on the platform continues to be very strong, 
across InstaHelp and Core. I think people will always want to join, be part of a formal 
workforce, have a dignified life, have access to middle-class earnings, as well as all the 
other benefits that we provide, in terms of life, health, and accidental insurance, access to 
credit, upskilling, etc. So there's definitely — across the two segments, the top of the funnel 
is not the challenge. 
I think the challenge is: can you identify the right people, who have the customer-centricity, 
the sincerity to work with purpose, who see a long-term pathway on the platform? And 
then, do you invest correctly in the training and onboarding, and setting them up for 
success, and then, over their lifecycle, are you able to support them well, so that they get 
retained, and their earnings grow, and their overall ratings and reputation on the platform 
compound? I think that's what this whole business is about, and that's where our focus is. 
It's easy to add bodies in this business — it's hard to retain the right supply and maintain a 
very low partner churn. And I think some of these things tend to play out in the medium 
term. So that's where we are focused on. 
On take rates, I think eventually experts care about net income in their hand — that's what 
they really care about. They look at: hey, I'm committing a certain amount of time to the 
platform, what is my absolute earnings? So it's less about take rate for services, it's more 
about absolute earnings. And there, we feel we are very competitive, as a function of 
densification, as a function of our brand, as a function of the scale that we have. And we 
will continue to work harder and harder to ensure that the earnings on the platform remain 
best-in-class. 
On the second point, on the steady-state picture of InstaHelp — I think we do have a view, 
and a very clear view there, and we continue to see if our older micro-markets are tracking 
towards that view. Without getting into the nitty-gritties of that view, at the highest level, as 
I have mentioned on a few earlier calls as well, we will need the pricing to reach roughly 
about ₹200 an hour, and the net order value to reach roughly about ₹300, given the average 
order is about one-and-a-half hours. 
This is because our view is that, even with the best utilization, you need about ₹150 an hour
